one_liner: C99 rewrite of the Bitshuffle bit-transpose filter with SSE2/AVX2/AVX-512/GFNI kernels; claims 1.3x-10x over classic bitshuffle.
what_it_does: Implements only the core Bitshuffle block transform: bitshuf_encode_block transposes the bits of a block of fixed-size elements so that bit k of every element lands in one contiguous plane, and bitshuf_decode_block inverts it; the output is meant to be fed to LZ4/Zstd. The API takes out, in, a caller-owned scratch buffer (same size as the block, required for elem_size > 1), an element count that must be a multiple of 8, and elem_size; it returns 0 or -1. It produces the same output as kiyo-masui's bshuf_trans_bit_elem/bshuf_untrans_bit_elem but with a different signature and argument order, and it has no blocking, compression, HDF5 or Python layer.
how_it_is_fast: Encode is a byte transpose (element bytes into byte planes, with specialised kernels for 2, 4 and 8 byte elements) followed by an 8x8 bit-matrix transpose on each plane; decode runs the same steps in reverse. The bit transpose uses movemask-style SIMD kernels for SSE2, AVX2 and AVX-512BW, plus an AVX-512VBMI+GFNI kernel that does the 8x8 bit transpose with a GF(2) affine instruction (vgf2p8affineqb) after a VBMI byte permute. Kernels are picked at load time with GNU IFUNC resolvers (__builtin_cpu_supports), so one binary uses the best ISA. The library never allocates; the classic implementation mallocs a temporary buffer of the full block size on every call, which also accounts for part of the measured gain on small blocks.
when_to_use: You already bitshuffle typed numeric arrays (float32/float64/int16 sensor, image or simulation data) before LZ4/Zstd and the transpose shows up in profiles.
x86-64 Linux with GCC 8+ or Clang 8+ servers, where IFUNC dispatch picks AVX2, AVX-512BW or AVX-512VBMI+GFNI (Ice Lake, Zen 4/5) at run time from one build.
Hot loops over many small blocks (the benchmark covers 256 B to 16 KB), where avoiding the classic library's per-call malloc matters.
You need a tiny dependency: one .c and one .h file, C89/C++-compatible header, dual MIT/Apache-2.0, easy to vendor.
when_not_to_use: aarch64/ARM: there is no NEON kernel, so non-x86 targets get the portable scalar Hacker's Delight transpose8, while classic bitshuffle 0.5.1 has a NEON path; it may be slower there (not documented, and CI runs the arm64 benchmark but publishes no numbers).
Big-endian targets: the build stops with #error, and support is not planned.
You need the full Bitshuffle format (blocked framing, built-in LZ4/Zstd, HDF5 filter 32008, Python bindings): use kiyo-masui/bitshuffle, c-blosc2 or hdf5plugin instead.
You want maintained, widely used code: 5 commits, last one 2024-01-22, 7 stars, and no release tags.
Integer bit-width packing (FOR, varint, PFor) is the actual need: this is a compression pre-filter, not a bit packer.

integration.dependencies: none (Google Benchmark and GoogleTest only for the Bazel test and benchmark targets; the benchmark also pulls classic bitshuffle 0.5.1)
integration.min_toolchain: C99 compiler; IFUNC dispatch is on for GCC 8+ or Clang 8+ with the ifunc/target attributes and off for ICC and MSVC. CI covers GCC, Clang (libstdc++ and libc++) and MSVC 2019/2022. Build files are Bazel only (WORKSPACE, no CMake).
integration.platforms: Little-endian only. x86/x86-64 with SSE2, AVX2, AVX-512BW+VL and AVX-512VBMI+VL+GFNI kernels; other architectures (arm64 is tested in CI) fall back to scalar C. Linux, macOS and Windows are tested; without IFUNC (MSVC, macOS) the ISA is fixed at compile time by -m/arch flags.
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the functions keep no global state apart from IFUNC resolvers that run at load time, so concurrent calls with separate buffers look safe on reading the source
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: output is bit-identical to bshuf_trans_bit_elem/bshuf_untrans_bit_elem, but the signature differs (out first, explicit scratch buffer, int return) and there is no blocked bshuf_bitshuffle/compress wrapper

gotchas: Without IFUNC (MSVC, macOS, ICC, or BITSHUF_USE_IFUNC=0) the SIMD level is fixed by compiler flags; a default x86-64 build without -mavx2 or /arch:AVX2 uses only SSE2.

elem_size > 1 needs a scratch buffer of size*elem_size bytes, or the call returns -1. Buffers are restrict, so overlapping out/in/scratch is undefined behaviour. size*elem_size is not checked for overflow.

The encode resolver skips the AVX-512VBMI+GFNI kernel on Intel CPUs (it checks !__builtin_cpu_is("intel")) and uses AVX-512BW there, but the decode resolver does not; this tuning choice is not explained.

Benchmark fairness: the classic library in tests/bitshuffle_benchmark.cc is built with the same global copts, so it picks its ISA at compile time (AVX512/AVX2/SSE2/NEON macros), while this library dispatches at run time. A default -c opt build therefore compares AVX-512 or AVX2 kernels here with classic SSE2; also, classic allocates per call.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: None of the integer-packing siblings (FastPFor, simdcomp, TurboPFor, Stream VByte) do bit transposition of arbitrary-width typed data. Pick this when you want a Bitshuffle pre-filter for float/int arrays ahead of a general compressor. Pick Sprintz or TurboPFor when you want a complete integer/time-series codec.
verified_claims_summary: The README claims a 1.3x to 10x speedup over classic bitshuffle 0.5.1's bshuf_trans_bit_elem/bshuf_untrans_bit_elem depending on CPU, function and arguments. The Google Benchmark harness (elem_size 1-18 and 63-66, blocks of 256 B to 256 MB, memcpy as reference) is public and CI runs it on self-hosted Ice Lake and arm64 machines at -O3 with GCC and Clang, but no result tables, CPU models or per-case numbers are published.
status_note: Stale since 2024-01-22 (5 commits, no releases), but it is a dual MIT/Apache-2.0 single-file C99 library with thorough CI (ASan/UBSan across SSE2-to-GFNI builds, MSVC, macOS, arm64) and exhaustive one-bit round-trip tests, so it is low-risk to vendor.
